newsitem.title: KENYA: FOCUS - Kenya shilling slides as foreigners buy dlrs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kenya shilling slides as foreigners buy dlrs.

text.p: Kenya's embattled shilling took a further beating on Monday on renewed demand for the dollar from foreign investors pulling out of a nervous market under siege from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), dealers said.

The shilling, which has undergone severe battering since the IMF halted a $205 million aid package 11 days ago, closed at a commercial mean rate of 70 to the dollar from Monday's opening at 68.87 -- a loss of 1.64 percent.
Some commercial banks quoted rates of up to 72 to the dollar.

The crisis in Kenya's money market worsened on Monday after weekend reports in local dailies that the World Bank was contemplating cutting off aid for vital programmes such as road building and repairs.
The privately owned Sunday Nation said the Bank had before the IMF decision already delayed disbursement of up to $71 million in Structural Adjustment Credit and other projects.
Political violence on Friday which left four people dead, including two policemen, further eroded market confidence, analysts said.
The violence was sparked by a national strike called by opposition leaders and activists demanding constitutional reforms before general elections due to be held later this year.

Market analysts said only strong positive signals from both the Fund and the government of President Daniel arap Moi could help calm a volatile market but Moi sent jitters into the market last week when he played down the signifance of IMF aid.
Commercial bank dealers said the shilling looked bleak as foreign investors rushed to sell treasury bills.
"The market today is clearly one-sided. There is some good demand from offshore investors," a senior dealer from a leading commercial bank told Reuters.
"It's a combination. Most still want to get out while others are taking positions because they think the shilling will weaken more," he added.
The shilling sunk to a new official record low against the dollar of 70.26 on Thursday at the end of a five-day slide since the IMF moved to rein in runaway corruption in this east African country.

At the centre of the IMF-Kenya standoff is a massive multi-million dollar gold and diamond scam involving a local firm, Goldenberg International, and senior civil servants and politically-connected individuals.
Kenya produces little gold and no diamonds but Moi's treasury still managed to pay out about $100 million taxpayers's money to Goldenberg.

Market analysts said the major reason for the shilling's slide was a loss in confidence by foreign investors, who no longer sure of the country's economic stability, were getting out at whatever price.
"It's not so much the fact that we lost the money but that we were blacklisted by the IMF, and investors use the IMF credit rating to determine where they will take their money," one analyst said.
Dealers said they were getting orders of upto $20 million and that at high prices -- 70.50 -- 71.50.
"Today there are no local orders. It's all from offshore investors and I don't think the local market (interbank) can support it," a senior dealer from a foreign bank told Reuters.
On Friday, the shilling picked up marginally as exporters sold dollars following the shilling record fall.
